extracted.intended_audience: Congressional staff, policymakers, and federal agency officials overseeing or implementing competitive sourcing/outsourcing (OMB A-76/FAIR) policies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for determining when recurring federal commercial activities should be performed in-house or transferred to the private sector via managed competitions under OMB Circular A-76 and the FAIR Act, with related procedural, reporting, and challenge rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a commercial activity
rubrics_metrics.description: A commercial activity is one that is a result of a requirement, or need, that the federal government has for a product or service, and that the product or service could be obtained from a private sector source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'recurring' commercial activity is one required by the federal government on a consistent, long-term basis. The Circular provides guidance and procedures for determining whether recurring commercial activities should be performed by private sector sources, government sources, or through inter-service support agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of inherently governmental functions (OFPP guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inherently governmental functions are 'those so intimately related to the exercise of the public interest as to mandate performance by federal employees.' They include activities that require exercise of discretion in applying Government authority or making value judgments in decisions for the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (OFPP Letter 92-1): (a) bind the United States to take or not take action by contract, policy, regulation, authorization, order, or otherwise; (b) determine, protect, and advance U.S. economic, political, territorial, property or other interests by military/diplomatic action, judicial proceedings, contract management, or otherwise; (c) significantly affect life, liberty, or property of private persons; (d) commission, appoint, direct, or control officers or employees of the United States; (e) exert ultimate control over acquisition, use, or disposition of U.S. property including collection/disbursement of appropriated funds. Inherently governmental functions do not normally include gathering information, providing advice/recommendations, or primarily ministerial/internal functions (e.g., building security, mail operations, cafeterias, housekeeping, facilities ops/maintenance, warehouse operations, motor vehicle fleet operations, routine electrical/mechanical services). Any function not considered inherently governmental is commercial and subject to competitive outsourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency requirements when using A-76 (three-step requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal executive agencies are required to: (1) develop a performance work statement defining technical aspects of the work to be performed; (2) determine the Most Efficient Organization (MEO) using current government workforce by reexamining management structure, personnel requirements and procedures; and (3) when such a comparison is required, conduct cost comparison studies among all sectors including private, other public agencies, and the current government MEO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost-comparison studies are not required to convert certain activities to/from in-house operation, commercial contract, or inter-service support agreements. Agencies are not required to use A-76 but, if they do, must follow these procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of managed competitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Three types of managed competitions under the policy are: (1) public-public, (2) public-private, and (3) private-private.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitions are held between public agencies and the private commercial sectors to determine who can best perform the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeframes for completing competitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory/appropriations guidance directs that single-function competitions are to be completed within 24 months and multi-function competitions within 48 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically competitions have ranged from 18 months (smaller, single-function) to more than four years (multi-function); GAO reports average multi-function studies since 1991 have taken about 30 months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy assumptions underlying A-76
rubrics_metrics.description: The policy rests on these assumptions: (1) the federal government should not compete against its citizens but rely on the commercial sector; (2) the government can conduct cost comparison studies to determine 'who best to do the work' through 'managed competitions'; (3) market forces can determine the most effective and cost-efficient methods to operate functions; (4) competition in the marketplace can be 'self-managed' and not require government oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These assumptions frame when and why agencies should use A-76-managed competitions; objections and critiques often address these assumptions directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost comparison / overhead and pricing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The government routinely assigns a 12-13% administrative and overhead cost rate to federal agencies when competing for contracts; to win a competition, outside proposals must be at least 10% less than the MEO’s proposals (per A-76 practice described).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argue the 12-13% overhead rate underestimates true infrastructure costs (IT community often uses ~40%), giving government an advantage. See A-76 Supplemental Handbook discussion of preparing in-house and contract cost estimates and GAO review of overhead rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct conversion and cost-comparison waivers
rubrics_metrics.description: The A-76 Supplemental Handbook allows for direct conversion to a private sector contractor and cost-comparison waivers to the A-76 policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal or procedural challenges to the policy or procedures are provided for in the Supplemental Handbook; updated versions available on OMB website.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAIR Act annual inventory requirement and schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the FAIR Act, federal executive agencies are required to submit to OMB, by June 30 of each year, annual inventories (lists) of 'non-inherently governmental functions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventories will be made available to Congress and eventually published in the Federal Register. Agencies may argue for inclusions/exclusions; initial submissions require more analysis; OMB will review and consult with agency heads and publish the lists 'within a reasonable time.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge and response process for FAIR inventories
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventories can be challenged by 'interested parties' as defined in the legislation. Once challenged, agencies must either accept the challenge, make changes to the list, or reject the challenge, and agree to do so within 30 days after the challenge is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-inventory response deadlines (e.g., Sept 30, 1999) and procedures have been used; challenges have come from private industry, unions, and other stakeholders. Agencies' handling of challenges may be subject to public scrutiny and legal remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to FAIR Act coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions include, but are not limited to, the General Accounting Office, government corporations or 'government-controlled corporations,' non-appropriated fund instrumentalities, and certain depot-level maintenance and repair organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative text (FAIR Act) enumerates specific exceptions; agencies should verify applicability when preparing inventories.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB and Congressional oversight responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB will review agency inventories and consult with agency heads; Congress can exercise oversight by monitoring agency progress, determining whether cost savings are real, and granting agencies authority to explore alternatives to A-76.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congressional oversight includes ensuring agencies meet deadlines and report promptly, accurately, and completely; oversight is important because agencies may follow the letter but not the spirit of the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may conduct an inventory and impartiality concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may conduct their own inventories, but questions exist about whether agencies can fairly and accurately inventory their own activities; civilian agencies historically reported few A-76 studies and may prefer other management improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because agencies prepare their own lists, outsiders (contractors, other agencies) may lack a complete picture; congressional oversight and opportunities to challenge lists aim to provide impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protest and legal remedies for aggrieved bidders
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggrieved bidders may seek legal remedies when they believe competitions or inventory determinations were improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not handled expeditiously, legal challenges could lengthen procurement cycles, generate federal rule-making, and empower courts/regulatory agencies to provide greater oversight of procurement processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of poor contracting/competition practice (audit findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: DOD Inspector General audits found recurring problems in contract actions: non-use of prior history to define requirements, inadequate government cost estimates, cursory technical reviews, inadequate competition, failure to award multiple-award contracts, inadequate price negotiation memorandums, inadequate contract surveillance, and lack of cost control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These problems indicate weak management of service contracts and can reduce expected savings from outsourcing; agencies should address these areas to improve outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of projected cost savings and accounting for competition costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Savings projections must account for the costs of conducting competitions and realistic timelines; GAO concluded DOD’s estimates may have overstated savings because they did not fully calculate investment costs and competition timeframes were longer than projected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should include start-up and execution costs of competitions, and realistic schedule estimates, when projecting net savings; failure to do so can mislead budget decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of essential organic capabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Some organic, technical capability should be retained within the federal government to support unique requirements (e.g., specialized computerized engineering, nuclear propulsion capability), though the exact amount is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinations of what must remain in-house should consider mission-critical, unique capabilities and national security implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concerns for national security and safety-sensitive functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Outsourcing safety- or security-sensitive activities (e.g., weapons handling) raises special concerns: potential compromise of national security, reduced worker training, threat of strikes, lack of oath/loyalty, and contractor decisions driven by cost/efficiency rather than mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions that could affect operational capabilities or safety may warrant exclusion from outsourcing or special oversight requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative approaches to A-76 (strategic sourcing and in-house restructuring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatives include strategic sourcing, allowing services to reorganize or modify federal jobs and retain them without managed competitions, and exploring re-engineering, consolidation, termination of inefficient practices, and other streamlined business practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While alternatives can increase flexibility and may be more time-efficient, critics caution that without cost/benefit analysis, outsourcing decisions could be arbitrary and lack competitive justification.
